title: A Journey through States of Water
intro: Water is the only common substance you can see in three forms in everyday life — solid, liquid, and gas. This chapter follows water on its journey through these states and explains how it travels round and round in the water cycle.

sections.heading: Three States of Water
bullets: Ice is solid water — it has a fixed shape and feels hard.
Water in a glass is liquid — it takes the shape of the container and flows easily.
Water vapour is gaseous water — it has no shape and spreads to fill any space.
All three are the same chemical substance; only the way the tiny particles arrange themselves changes.
In ice, particles are packed tightly; in water they are close but free to slide; in vapour they fly far apart.

sections.heading: Changing State
bullets: Melting: solid ice turns to liquid water when heated. This happens at 0 °C.
Freezing: liquid water turns to solid ice when cooled to 0 °C.
Evaporation: liquid water slowly turns to vapour at any temperature; faster on hot days, in wind, and over a wide surface.
Boiling: liquid water turns rapidly to vapour at 100 °C.
Condensation: water vapour cools and turns back into tiny droplets — that's how clouds and the water on a cold glass are formed.
Heat is added to melt or evaporate; heat is taken away to freeze or condense.

sections.heading: Water Vapour in the Air
bullets: Air around us always has some water vapour mixed in; the amount is called humidity.
Dew on grass in the morning is condensed water vapour from cool night air.
Fog is tiny water droplets hanging close to the ground when air cools rapidly.
When you breathe out on a cold day, the warm vapour from your breath quickly condenses into a small white cloud.
Wet clothes dry because water in them evaporates into the surrounding air.

sections.heading: The Water Cycle
bullets: The Sun heats up oceans, lakes, rivers, and even moist soil; water evaporates into vapour.
Vapour rises high into the cool sky and condenses into tiny droplets, forming clouds.
When droplets join into bigger ones, they fall as rain (or snow, hail) — this is precipitation.
Some rainwater flows back into rivers and seas; some seeps into the ground.
From rivers, oceans, and soil, water again evaporates — and the cycle continues without end.

sections.heading: Why Water Matters
bullets: Every living thing — plant, animal, human — needs water to stay alive.
We use water for drinking, cooking, washing, farming, and making things in factories.
Less than 1% of all water on Earth is fresh and ready to drink.
Polluting water with chemicals or sewage harms us and other living things.
Saving water means turning off taps, fixing leaks, and reusing greywater for plants.

sections.heading: Rainwater Harvesting and Conservation
bullets: Rainwater harvesting collects rain from rooftops into tanks or recharge pits.
Stored rainwater can be used for gardening, washing, flushing, and even drinking after treatment.
Recharge pits let rainwater seep back underground, raising the water table.
Planting trees, restoring lakes, and protecting wetlands all help keep water on the land.
Water saved today is water available tomorrow — for us, our farms, and other living things.

key_takeaways: Water exists in three states — solid, liquid, and gas — and we see all three in daily life.
Melting, freezing, evaporation, and condensation are changes of state caused by adding or removing heat.
Water vapour in air explains dew, fog, and clouds.
In the water cycle, water evaporates, condenses, falls as rain, and flows back to the sea.
Less than 1% of Earth's water is fresh and usable, so saving and protecting water is essential.
Rainwater harvesting and conservation steps help maintain the water cycle for future generations.

glossary.definition: A state of matter with fixed shape and tightly packed particles, like ice.
A state of matter that flows and takes the shape of its container.
A state of matter that has no fixed shape or volume; particles spread to fill any space.
Change from solid to liquid when heat is added.
Change from liquid to solid when heat is removed.
The slow change of liquid to gas at the surface, even below boiling.
The rapid change of liquid to gas throughout the liquid, at boiling point.
Change from gas back to liquid when vapour cools.
The continuous movement of water — evaporate, condense, fall as rain, flow back.
The amount of water vapour present in the air.
Collecting rainwater from rooftops or surfaces for later use.
